why_the_container_was_stopped.explanation: The court was started at 15:57 EST during the short pre-reboot uptime and was still running when that uptime ended at 16:04:41 EST. The container is --restart=no, so the host reboot ended it. dockerd itself did not come back after the reboot because docker.service is unit-file 'disabled' (preset: disabled) and nothing had connected to the socket-activation unit, so it stayed inactive until this session started docker.socket. On daemon restore dockerd stamped the prior run with ExitCode=255 ('Restoring containers' could not recover a state that was never cleanly stopped) and logged 'error unmounting container ... layer not mounted' for the restored container. 255 here is the restart/restore code, not an OOM (OOMKilled=false, memory.events oom=0) and not an application exit.
why_the_container_was_stopped.gate_log_torn_by_the_same_reboot: court/freeze-b79/gates.log (15:45-15:58) ends mid `cargo test --lib` with no '=== exit=' line, and court/freeze-b79/clippy.time records 'sh: /usr/bin/time: No such file or directory'. The previous gate run therefore produced no usable result and was re-run from scratch in this session; the torn log is preserved as court/freeze-b79/gates-b79-interrupted.log.

It is applied because the user explicitly authorized it, and it is recorded here as a deviation to be reviewed, never as compliance. The 16 CPU quota likewise exceeds the wrapper's default --cpus=8.
compliance_statement.why_the_risk_is_bounded: The host has 41 GiB available and 45 GiB of unused swap, the container's swap allowance is pinned to 0 (memory.swap.max=0) so exceeding 16 GiB produces an in-container OOM kill instead of host-wide pressure, oom_score_adj=500 makes the disposable court the kernel's preferred victim, and one heavy command runs at a time with CARGO_BUILD_JOBS=8 / --test-threads=4.
